entries.title: Apply phase-52 consumer payment authority (after phases 49, 50 and 51)
entries.authorizedBy: Roger Roman (Phase 52 directive: anon and authenticated cannot insert or update any payment fact; all legitimate payment writes move to a server-only admin/webhook path) — repository integration only
entries.why: Terminal B proved the phase-51 gate is bypassable by the payer it charges (audit commit f82f842, RCAP-SEC-001). Four failures: an authenticated participant wrote payment_status='paid' and amount_cents=5000 on their own row and opened delivery (G1/G1b), because the phase-26 RLS UPDATE policy scopes rows and not columns; one paid item authorized a second distinct matter (G11), because the consumption unit hashed the render job id and every new job is a new id; and participant B's paid item authorized a job for participant A (G12), because the probe took an item id and never asked who owned it. This migration makes payment facts unwritable by the payer, moves legitimate writes to a server-only path with unique provider evidence, rekeys consumption onto the Briefcase item and the provider receipt, and binds every consumer job to an immutable item, consumer, person and matter.
entries.riskNote: Additive and forward-only: no table is dropped, no row is backfilled, and the partner branch of finalize_packet_render_job is unchanged, so sponsored accounting is untouched. The change is restrictive in two directions that matter operationally. First, anon and authenticated lose INSERT and UPDATE on the payment columns of consumer_briefcase_items; any application code that writes payment_status, amount_cents or the checkout metadata directly from a participant session will start failing with permission denied and must move to record_consumer_packet_payment. Second, an unsponsored job is now deliverable only when it carries the full four-tuple, so consumer jobs enqueued before this phase — which have no consumer_auth_user_id — fail closed rather than delivering. That is the intended direction, but it is a behaviour change on existing queued work and is why this is medium rather than low.

entries.title: Harden public.rcap_persons and enforce the reserved direct-to-consumer person namespace
entries.authorizedBy: Roger Roman — explicit bounded authorization for an additive Phase 54: inspect and record current privileges, enable RLS on public.rcap_persons, revoke direct anon and authenticated access, preserve narrowly required server-side access, add a database-enforced reserved-namespace collision guard, update legitimate callers, add executable role/tenant/reporting/entitlement/attribution/namespace-isolation tests, exact-path SHA-pinned repository authorization, ephemeral local application for testing only
entries.why: rcap_persons carried no row-level security, no policies and no explicit grants anywhere in supabase/, so it inherited whatever default privileges hand anon and authenticated. That predates the consumer namespace and was already wrong for partner intake identities; Phase 53's consumer binding put direct-to-consumer person rows in the same table and made it urgent. Two further gaps had no database enforcement at all: partner_slug is free text, so a real partner could register the reserved slug and absorb every consumer person into their keyspace, and nothing constrained which identities may sit in the reserved namespace, leaving attribution ambiguous in both directions.
entries.riskNote: Privilege-removing rather than additive in effect, which is the risk worth naming: if any caller read rcap_persons as anon or authenticated it would break. Every caller in src/ uses the service-role admin client (source-repository.ts, rcap-intake/repository.ts, consumer-identity.ts, and the partner outcome summary), and service_role is BYPASSRLS, so the revoke removes no access anything relies on. Verified by R6, a positive control proving the sanctioned server-side path still reads and writes after the lockdown.

entries.title: Public-view and default-privilege hardening (Security Advisor remediation)
entries.why: Codifies the Security Advisor remediation validated in the legalease-rcap-acceptance project: row level security on partner_entitlement, rcap_record_events and the two acceptance tables where they exist; security_invoker on the five content_public_* views with anon RLS policies and column-level grants that reproduce their published row sets exactly; and withdrawal of the baseline default privileges that grant anon and authenticated everything on every future object in public. Nothing here is authorized for Production execution.
entries.riskNote: The change is additive to the security posture and removes no existing access: no policy is dropped, no privilege authenticated already holds is revoked, and every anon grant it adds is column-level on a table whose RLS admits only rows the public views already returned. The one behavioural change a reviewer must weigh is that a security_invoker view checks column privileges for the columns it filters on, so anon can read is_active, status, published_at, archived, approved and content_posts.updated_at for rows that are already public.
entries.rollback: Forward-only in the chain, reversible by statement: re-set the five views to security_definer (alter view ... reset (security_invoker)), drop the six *_anon_public_read policies, revoke the 64 column grants, and re-issue the six ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES grants the baseline carried. Nothing is dropped or rewritten, so no data recovery is involved. Local rehearsal is scripts/rcap-schema-upgrade-lab.sh build stacked-pre, which builds the pre-remediation schema from the same sources.

entries.title: RCAP partner provisioning and existing-user administrator claim
entries.authorizedBy: Roger Roman — owner authorization in the RCAP partner provisioning and existing-user admin claim assignment, 2026-08-19
entries.why: Provisioning a partner tenant was a sequence of writes with no rollback, and with the Phase 1 onboarding flag on there was no path to create a partner at all. Eleven restricted paths carry the fix. The migration adds one forward-only transactional function, rcap_service_provision_partner, plus a deterministic id helper; it creates no table, drops nothing, revokes execution from public, anon and authenticated, grants it only to service_role, and pins search_path to '' on both functions. The internal provisioning route is the single authorized HTTP entry point and contains no write of its own. The two claim paths and the setup route let an invited email that already belongs to exactly one confirmed Auth user accept through the ordinary sign-in instead of a password-recovery link, and render the designed recovery states when it cannot. The remaining library paths are the provisioning domain and service, the first-admin domain and service, the claim-cookie contract, and one added route helper. The path set is the union of every restricted-path guard in the repository: source-engine-change-scope.mjs treats supabase/ and the two claim routes as restricted, while verify-expungement-consumer-adapter.mjs additionally treats all of src/lib/partners/ and src/app/partner/ as restricted, so every one of them is named here rather than only those the narrower guard would catch.
entries.riskNote: The migration is additive and creates no schema object beyond two functions, so nothing existing can be rejected or lost by applying it. The behavioural change a reviewer must weigh is the new claim path: a pending first-admin invitation is now carried through sign-in in an HttpOnly, one-hour cookie holding the one-time token, and is consumed only after the live session's email matches the invitation exactly. A wrong signed-in email is refused before any record changes and the invitation stays usable by the named administrator. Nothing here publishes, activates, creates an access code, or touches billing. A provisioned tenant is also not trivially deletable, because the onboarding activity trail is append-only; a reviewer should treat provisioning as a decision to keep a private record, not a scratch action.
entries.rollback: Forward-only in the chain, reversible by statement: drop function public.rcap_service_provision_partner(text, text, text, text, text, text, text, text, uuid, uuid, text, text) and public.rcap_partner_page_configuration_id(text). No table, column, policy, grant or row created by the baseline is altered, so no data recovery is involved. The application paths revert by reverting the commits, which restores the previous first-admin flow. Removing an already-provisioned tenant is NOT an ordinary cascade: partner_onboarding_activity carries a BEFORE DELETE trigger that refuses every row, so a delete on partner_records fails on the workspace's own activity record. Removal requires a privileged session that clears partner_onboarding_activity for that workspace first. That is a pre-existing property of every onboarding workspace, not something this change introduces, and a provisioned tenant left in place is private, inactive, unbilled and unreachable from the public route.
evidence: node scripts/verify-rcap-partner-provisioning.mjs — 33/33 checks: one canonical provisioning implementation, transaction and idempotency guarantees, private and inactive initial state, no access code or billing side effect, internal-only invocation, both invitation paths, no duplicate Auth user, no password recovery, exact-email claim, wrong-email denial, replay prevention, expired and revoked recovery, canary dry-run default and exact Production confirmations
